questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Horizontal Asymptote When the Degree of the Numerator is Greater
questions.worked_solution:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is $x.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by $x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2{x}^{2}+x+6}{x-1} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2{x}^{2}}{x}+\frac{x}{x}+\frac{6}{x})}{(\frac{x}{x}-\frac{1}{x})} \\  & =\frac{(2x+1+\frac{6}{x})}{(1-\frac{1}{x})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{6}{x}$ and $\frac{1}{x}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(2x+1+\frac{6}{x})}{(1-\frac{1}{x})} \\  & ≈\frac{2x+1+0}{1-0} \\  & =\frac{2x+1}{1} \\  & =2x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

This is not a constant, which means that $y=f(x)$ does not have a horizontal asymptote.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Horizontal Asymptote When the Degree of the Denominator is Greater
questions.problem: Determine the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}-1}{3{x}^{4}-x+3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{4}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{4},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}-1}{3{x}^{4}-x+3} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{4}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{4}})}{(\frac{3{x}^{4}}{{x}^{4}}-\frac{x}{{x}^{4}}+\frac{3}{{x}^{4}})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{4}})}{(3-\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{3}{{x}^{4}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},\frac{1}{{x}^{4}},\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}$ and $\frac{3}{{x}^{4}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{4}})}{(3-\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{3}{{x}^{4}})} \\  & \to \frac{0-0}{3-0+0} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y=0.$

questions.problem: Determine the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x)=\frac{7x+3}{6{x}^{7}-2{x}^{2}-1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{7}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{7},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{7x+3}{6{x}^{7}-2{x}^{2}-1} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{7x}{{x}^{7}}+\frac{3}{{x}^{7}})}{(\frac{6{x}^{7}}{{x}^{7}}-\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{7}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{7}})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{7}{{x}^{6}}+\frac{3}{{x}^{7}})}{(6-\frac{2}{{x}^{5}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{7}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{7}{{x}^{6}},\frac{3}{{x}^{7}},\frac{2}{{x}^{5}}$ and $\frac{1}{{x}^{7}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(\frac{7}{{x}^{6}}+\frac{3}{{x}^{7}})}{(6-\frac{2}{{x}^{5}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{7}})} \\  & \to \frac{0+0}{6-0-0} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y=0.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Horizontal Asymptote When the Degree of the Numerator is Greater
questions.worked_solution:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{6}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{6},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{8}-4{x}^{4}+2x}{{x}^{6}-1} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{x}^{8}}{{x}^{6}}-\frac{4{x}^{4}}{{x}^{6}}+\frac{2x}{{x}^{6}})}{(\frac{{x}^{6}}{{x}^{6}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{6}})} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}-\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{2}{{x}^{5}})}{(1-\frac{1}{{x}^{6}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{4}{{x}^{2}},$ $\frac{2}{{x}^{5}}$ and $\frac{1}{{x}^{6}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{({x}^{2}-\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{2}{{x}^{5}})}{(1-\frac{1}{{x}^{6}})} \\  & ≈\frac{{x}^{2}-0+0}{1-0} \\  & ={x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is not a constant, which means that $y=f(x)$ does not have a horizontal asymptote.

To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{4}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{4},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{8{x}^{6}+3{x}^{2}-7}{{x}^{4}-6x} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{8{x}^{6}}{{x}^{4}}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{{x}^{4}}-\frac{7}{{x}^{4}})}{(\frac{{x}^{4}}{{x}^{4}}-\frac{6x}{{x}^{4}})} \\  & =\frac{(8{x}^{2}+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{7}{{x}^{4}})}{(1-\frac{6}{{x}^{3}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{3}{{x}^{2}},$ $\frac{7}{{x}^{4}}$ and $\frac{6}{{x}^{3}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(8{x}^{2}+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{7}{{x}^{4}})}{(1-\frac{6}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & ≈\frac{8{x}^{2}+0-0}{1-0} \\  & =8{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This is not a constant, which means that $y=f(x)$ does not have a horizontal asymptote.
